Trump descended the stairs from his plane to be met by Xi, as well as renditions of both countries’ national anthems and fighter jets that flew overhead and left colorful vapour trails.
The pair strolled down a red carpet lined with people waving pom-poms, brandishing Chinese and US national flags, and shouting: “A warm welcome to you!”
A motorcade of dark limousines later carried Trump into the city, where the streets had been cleared of traffic, an AFP reporter observed.
Xi, Trump, Putin and other leaders attending the broader Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit then gathered for a welcome dinner, and the three briefly exchanged greetings before a group photo.
“I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape, with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations,” Xi told Trump, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Washington had signalled that the Ukraine war -- something Xi vehemently sees as not China’s problem -- was not expected to be addressed in the trilateral meeting, before Trump said that it would.
The summit is expected to include discussions of the Iran war and nuclear disarmament, according to Washington, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.
Beijing has long maintained that the US and Russia should reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.
Earlier on Wednesday, Putin struck a defiant tone on his war in Ukraine, saying Western sanctions provoked by the 2022 invasion had “failed.”
Addressing the Apec gathering, the Russian leader said he expected the trilateral summit to be “highly useful.”
“At a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division... and dialogue rather than ultimatums,” Putin said.
The Russian leader has been largely shunned by the West since his 2022 offensive in Ukraine began, but has found an audience with Trump.
However, “full-scale” talks solely between Putin and Trump are unlikely to take place during their visits to China, Moscow said, according to Russian state media.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, also in Shenzhen, said sanctions would “continue to increase as long as this war goes on.”
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga, speaking to reporters in Kyiv, said he hoped Xi and Trump would put “pressure on Russia to end the war.”
Putin and Xi met, their fifth tete-a-tete this year, including one by video link. The two men have long touted their strong personal friendship.
Xi urged yet closer ties with Moscow, saying the nations should “leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties.”
Trump came to China from the Philippines, where a day earlier he met fellow leaders of the Quad -- Australia, Japan and India -- for the first time in his second term.
The grouping is broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence.
Trump has also floated the possibility of meeting Kim Jong Un in China, saying the North Korean leader “would like” to meet, although there has been no confirmation from Pyongyang.
Trump was in the Philippines for a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) where there were protests against a US supply chain initiative.
The spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large over his recent travels.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s own expanding trade with Asean.
On Tuesday, a combative Trump doubled down, saying the United States would catch China in rare-earths production “within 10 months.”

item.title: UN expert: ICJ verdict on Myanmar could be ‘step towards justice’ for Rohingya
item.description:
As the International Court of Justice (ICJ) prepares to deliver its judgment in the genocide case against Myanmar, a UN human rights expert has said the decision could mark an important step towards justice for the Rohingya. She also warned that continuing violence and insecurity make their safe return from Bangladesh impossible at present.
Kelley E Currie, UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said the judgment in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar would be an important moment for the Rohingya, Myanmar and the international community.
“This decision represents a potential step away from that impunity, and a potential step towards accountability for the perpetrators and justice for the survivors and the victims,” she said at her end-of-mission press conference at the UN house in Dhaka on Wednesday.
“We hope this verdict will recognise these crimes, call them by their right name and put us on the path towards justice.”
The ICJ, the United Nations’ principal judicial organ, is scheduled to deliver its judgment at 10am on Thursday in The Hague.
The case concerns Myanmar’s alleged violations of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, commonly known as the Genocide Convention.
For the more than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, the judgment comes amid continuing uncertainty over whether conditions will ever allow them to return safely to their homes in Myanmar.
Currie said crimes committed against the Rohingya, including dispossession, denial of identity, forced displacement, torture, sexual violence and murder, “did not begin or end in 2017”. Too many perpetrators had escaped accountability, she said, and too many victims had been denied justice.
If the judgment recognised the crimes, all nations would have a duty to support its full implementation, she said.
“Regardless of the outcome, these survivors, their community and their supporters around the world will never stop demanding justice and fighting for an end to impunity. I stand with them,” she said.
Currie called on countries maintaining business and other forms of engagement with Myanmar’s military authorities to reconsider their involvement.
She argued that continued economic and other support could enable the authorities to sustain violence and displacement. She urged governments to use pressure, including sanctions and measures to restrict sources of support, to discourage such engagement.
She also called on regional and international actors to stop actions that contribute to violence against civilians and to press Myanmar’s authorities to end abuses.
In her written statement, Currie said the authorities in Naypyidaw bore primary responsibility for the current crisis.
“The path to peace in Myanmar does not run through Naypyidaw,” she said.
Currie urged Bangladesh and international partners to adopt a comprehensive approach to the Rohingya crisis. She warned that worsening insecurity in refugee camps, declining humanitarian assistance and continued conflict in Myanmar were undermining prospects for safe and dignified returns.
Bangladesh continues to host more than one million Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar who cannot return home safely because of the ongoing human rights and humanitarian crisis, she said.
Deadly attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure continue amid intense fighting, particularly in Rakhine State.
Rohingya and other marginalised communities also face repression and severe deprivation of their civil, political, economic and cultural rights in areas controlled by both the authorities in Naypyidaw and the Arakan Army.
“These conditions not only make safe, dignified, and durable returns impossible for Rohingya refugees but are making life inside Myanmar increasingly dangerous,” she said.
The situation has also made humanitarian assistance inside Rakhine State more difficult, while donor support continues to decline.
Currie said the budget for refugee assistance in Bangladesh had reached an all-time low even as the population requiring assistance was at an all-time high.
Currie noted that Bangladesh’s newly elected government had formed a special committee to develop a comprehensive strategy for the early, safe, voluntary and dignified return of Rohingya refugees and others to Myanmar.
The final strategy has not yet been released. Currie said its proposed priorities included:
During her November 11–18 visit, she met senior government officials in Dhaka and travelled to Cox’s Bazar, where she met refugees, community members and organisations working in the camps.
Currie said insecurity was a common concern among the refugees she met, particularly for women and children.
She recounted hearing from women and girls afraid to leave their homes, mothers worried that their children could be abducted, and men who felt powerless when they and their families were abused by thugs and criminals.
She also raised concerns about precarious shelter for people who had arrived since 2024 and the vulnerabilities faced by religious minorities within the Rohingya community.
Insecurity and lawlessness, combined with a lack of meaningful economic and educational opportunities, were driving harmful coping strategies among refugees and host communities. These included drug use and trafficking, smuggling, human trafficking, recruitment into criminal or armed groups, and online gambling, she said.
Currie called for urgent improvements in camp security, including the removal, disarmament and disincentivisation of unauthorised armed actors, whether armed groups or criminal organisations.
She warned that recent donor cuts, particularly to protection, education, livelihoods and non-emergency healthcare, had worsened the situation.
“Further reductions in support risk creating a generation of young people with no hope and nothing to lose,” she said.
Currie cautioned that localisation of humanitarian assistance must not become an excuse for further funding cuts. Instead, it should involve strengthening local institutions, investing in the capacities of refugee and host communities, improving social cohesion and reforming camp management to ensure greater refugee representation and participation.
Currie described Myanmar’s conflict as part of a decades-long struggle over the country’s future. She contrasted an exclusionary state dominated by a military elite with the prospect of a federal democracy that respects the rights and dignity of all communities.
Inclusive political dialogue involving the Rohingya and other marginalised groups was essential to resolving the crisis, she said. She urged regional countries and other UN member states to support meaningful engagement among key stakeholders and to refrain from actions that contribute to violence against civilians.
She also called for a shift away from a charity-based approach that treats refugees merely as beneficiaries, towards a rights-based approach recognising them as people entitled to participate in decisions about their future.
Currie, who has been denied entry to Myanmar, said she would develop more detailed recommendations for relevant stakeholders. She will present a full report on her Bangladesh visit at the March 2027 session of the UN Human Rights Council.

item.title: Ex-state minister Hiru, two others sent to jail
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Wednesday sent former state minister for water resources Lt Col (retd) Mohammad Nazrul Islam Hiru and two others to jail in an Anti-Terrorism Act case filed with Banani Police Station.
The other accused are Kazi Mostafizul Islam Mukta and Barrister Rana Tajuddin Khan.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque passed the order following a petition by the investigation officer, Inspector Mohammad Abul Matin of the Detective Branch of police.
During the hearing, state lawyer Shamsuddoha Sumon argued in favour of showing the accused arrested and sought their detention. Defence lawyer Khaleda Jahan Lily opposed the move and sought bail.
She told the court that one of the accused, a Bir Protik award recipient, was elderly and had returned home from Combined Military Hospital (CMH) two days earlier after receiving treatment. However, the court did not hear the bail petition as the case documents were unavailable.
According to the case statement, a group of 100 to 120 people staged a torch procession on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway opposite the Army Stadium in Banani around 12:20am on August 7.
The processionists allegedly chanted slogans demanding the withdrawal of the ban on the activities of the Awami League and its associate organisation, Chhatra League, and the release of political prisoners.
Police arrested seven people in connection with the incident and seized 70 partially burnt torches, a banner and 70 black masks from the scene, the complaint said.
The investigation officer told the court that information obtained from the three accused was being scrutinised. Further interrogation might be necessary to identify and arrest other suspects and establish the circumstances of the incident.
The officer also expressed concern that the accused could hamper the investigation or go into hiding if released on bail, seeking their detention until the investigation is completed.

item.title: Arson attack on BNP office in Netrokona, nearby shop gutted
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to the BNP office of Chiram union in Barhatta upazila of Netrokona early Wednesday, destroying the office and an adjacent firewood shop.
The fire broke out at around 4am at Bamangaon Bazar in Chiram union, according to police and local sources.
A group of miscreants allegedly set fire to the union BNP office, and the flames quickly spread to the neighbouring firewood shop.
On information, firefighters rushed to the scene and brought the blaze under control. By then, both the office and the shop had been gutted.
Barhatta police station Officer-in-Charge Champak Dam told Dhaka Tribune that the initial suspicion was that miscreants had deliberately set fire to the office.
He said the adjacent shop was also damaged in the fire, adding that those involved had yet to be identified.
The police officer said the incident was being investigated and legal action would be taken accordingly.

item.title: Garment worker stabbed 29 times in 30 seconds in Mirpur
item.description:
A female garment worker was critically injured after a man allegedly attacked her with a sharp weapon, striking her 29 times in around 30 seconds, in Dhaka’s Mirpur on Wednesday.
The attack took place around 12:56pm on Road 5 in the Shialbari area of Rupnagar as the worker, identified as Nupur, was returning home during her lunch break.
CCTV footage shows several female workers walking along the road when a man suddenly approached Nupur from behind and began hacking her. Even after she fell to the ground, he continued the assault. A few people initially moved towards her but backed away, while others watched from nearby.
Police said the attack stemmed from a personal dispute and that a suspect had been arrested. Nupur is receiving treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
Additional Commissioner (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police Shafiqul Islam said both Nupur and the suspect, identified as Raihan, worked at a factory under the Rising Group.
They had been in a relationship, which reportedly ran into trouble, prompting the attack, he said, adding that the incident was not related to the ongoing garment workers' unrest.
The attack came amid tensions in Mirpur and Kafrul, where garment workers clashed with local BNP activists following allegations that female workers had been harassed.
Workers from Load Star Fashion and Mid Asia Fashion reportedly engaged in chases and exchanged brickbats with local political activists. Police said workers from the two factories had earlier disrupted production at nearby factories and brought their workers out.
Clashes were also reported in Mirpur-12, where police fired tear gas and sound grenades to disperse workers attempting to block roads.

item.title: Lawyer beaten at court premises sent to jail
item.description:
A pro-Awami League lawyer and Jubo League leader who was beaten by an agitated crowd on the court premises has been sent to jail along with two others in a case over a crude bomb explosion outside the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) Court in Dhaka.
The three accused — Advocate Dr Shamim Al Saiful Sohag, Obaidur Rahman Sudaich and Md Sumaiyaz Islam — were sent to jail on Wednesday after Dhaka Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Zakir Hossain rejected their bail petitions.
State lawyer Mohammad Shamsuddoha Sumon confirmed the order.
Police had produced the accused before the court and sought their detention in custody until the investigation was completed. The investigation officer, Sub-Inspector Anupam Das of Sutrapur Police Station, said they had admitted their involvement during preliminary interrogation.
Defence lawyers sought bail, while the prosecution opposed the petitions. Sohag, who is also a lawyer, told the court that he had been dragged out of a courtroom and assaulted by a crowd on Tuesday while attending a hearing in former Dhaka South City Corporation mayor Sayeed Khokon's remand case. He said he had been held for nearly an hour and lost consciousness during the assault.
“I came to court as a lawyer, but they turned me into an accused,” he told the court, denying any involvement in the November 9 explosion.
The prosecution argued that the accused were involved in the attack and opposed their release. The magistrate said police had found preliminary evidence linking them to the incident and noted that the case had been filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act, making bail inappropriate at this stage.
According to the case statement, crude bombs exploded near the main entrance of the CMM Court on the evening of November 9, creating panic. Around 25 to 30 unidentified people were allegedly involved, and two suspects were detained with the help of police and people present at the scene.
A case was filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act and Explosives Act by a Sutrapur police sub-inspector the following day.
Police later identified Sohag, Sudaich and Sumaiyaz as suspects based on the investigation. On Tuesday night, police took them into custody from an agitated crowd in front of Government Kabi Nazrul College in Sutrapur.
Sohag was injured in the crowd's assault and received treatment at Sir Salimullah Medical College Hospital.

item.title: Traffic police box set ablaze in Chittagong
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to a traffic police box in Muradpur, Chittagong, early Wednesday, prompting police to launch an investigation to identify those involved.
The incident took place around 1am. The fire failed to spread inside the box as its windows were closed, causing no major damage. No one was injured.
Police and local sources said several people set the box on fire before fleeing. Local residents later spotted the flames and brought the fire under control.
No police personnel were inside the box at the time. Officers learned about the incident in the morning.
Panchlaish Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mozammel Haque said police had collected CCTV footage and were examining it to identify those responsible.
He said the suspects had not yet been identified and legal action would be taken once they were traced.

item.title: Nearly 300 arrested as garment unrest flares in Savar, Ashulia
item.description:
Garment workers staged protests and clashed with police in several areas of Savar and Ashulia on Wednesday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. Police fired tear gas, sound grenades and rubber bullets to disperse demonstrators, leaving several people, including police personnel, injured.
Nearly 300 people have been arrested in 24 cases filed with Savar and Ashulia police stations over alleged acts of sabotage linked to the unrest, police said.
Most factories resumed production in the morning, but workers at several factories stopped work, while some attempted to block roads. At least 20 factories in Ashulia were closed on Wednesday, according to industrial police.
In Savar's Ulail area, workers from Al-Muslim and several other factories blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway around 2:30pm, bringing traffic to a standstill. Clashes broke out when industrial police reached the scene and workers allegedly threw bricks at them. Police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets. The workers withdrew from the highway around 4pm.
In Ashulia, workers attempted to block the Abdullahpur-Baipail road in Narsinghapur around 10:15am. Police chased them away and fired tear gas. Workers from nearby factories also allegedly attacked MK Apparels in Khejurbagan, damaging its gate, reception-area glass and a vehicle's windscreen.
Industrial police said 20 factories were closed, including some shut indefinitely under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act. Other factories declared general holidays, while production continued normally in many establishments.
Police also arrested two leaders of the Green Bangla Garments Workers Federation — its president Mosammat Sultana Begum and general secretary Md Ilias — from Pallabi in Dhaka on Tuesday night over allegations of inciting unrest and threatening factory owners and labour leaders. Local residents in Hemayetpur detained another labour leader, Humayun Kabir, and handed him over to police on Wednesday.
Police said the 24 cases filed in connection with the unrest had led to nearly 300 arrests.
Meanwhile, law enforcement agencies increased patrols and surveillance across the industrial belt to prevent further violence. The unrest came ahead of a nationwide shutdown program called by the activities-banned Awami League for Thursday.

item.title: 71 Awami League activists detained in Dhaka in 24 hours
item.description:
At least 71 activists and leaders of the activities-banned Awami League and its various affiliated organizations have been detained by police in Dhaka over the past 24 hours. Police said more than 2kg of gunpowder was recovered from a group of them.
The information was announced in a message sent by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Media Division.
According to police, the gunpowder had been collected from a border area and brought to Dhaka for sabotage through a post-holding leader of Meherpur Chhatra League.
Police said a small amount of the gunpowder was later ignited at a house in the Mirpur area to test its effectiveness.
After receiving information, detectives detained 3 activists and leaders of the Awami League and Chhatra League from the house, along with the gunpowder.

item.title: Tungipara violence: Police station, security vehicles, MP’s home torched overnight
item.description:
Tungipara in Gopalganj witnessed widespread violence overnight as protesters attacked a police station, set fire to security vehicles and torched at least 20 houses, including the residence of local lawmaker SM Zilani.
The violence was reportedly triggered by the arrest of several people on Tuesday night on suspicion of sabotage ahead of the activities-banned Awami League’s November 19 lockdown program.
According to local residents and eyewitnesses, loudspeaker announcements were made demanding the release of those arrested. Later, groups of protesters, including leaders and activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations, attacked Tungipara Police Station, vandalising and setting fire to the building.
The situation escalated when law enforcement agencies moved to bring the violence under control. Several people were injured in the ensuing clashes, including two reportedly hit by bullets, according to local sources.
Meanwhile, a BGB team reached Nilfa Bazar in Tungipara after reports of a road blockade. Clashes broke out between BGB members and protesters in several rounds.
Law enforcement personnel fired tear gas and sound grenades to disperse the crowds.
At one point, protesters allegedly set fire to several police vehicles, at least four police and BGB vehicles, and an armoured vehicle, local sources said.
At least 20 houses in the area were also reportedly set ablaze, including the residence of Gopalganj-3 MP SM Zilani.
A visit to different parts of Tungipara on Wednesday morning revealed signs of widespread destruction. No law enforcement personnel were seen in several areas, while tree trunks and electricity poles had been placed across roads to block traffic.
The blockades disrupted movement in different parts of the upazila.
In contrast, the situation in Gopalganj town remained largely normal despite a relatively limited presence of law enforcement personnel. Shops were open and traffic was moving normally.

item.title: RMG workers block Dhaka-Aricha highway over minimum wage demand
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway in Savar, demanding an increase in the minimum wage, prompting law enforcement agencies to fire tear gas to disperse them.
The protest began around 2:30pm on Wednesday when workers from several garment factories gathered on the highway, halting traffic and triggering severe congestion.
As of 3:20pm, the protesters were still occupying the highway and chanting slogans demanding fulfilment of their demands.
Savar Highway Police Station In-Charge Ali Ahmed said workers had taken to the highway over their minimum wage demand.
He said authorities were trying to bring the situation under control, persuade the workers to leave the road and restore normal traffic.

item.title: BNP parliamentary party meeting begins amid reports of violence
item.description:
The BNP parliamentary party on Wednesday afternoon held a meeting at the National Parliament Building amid reports of violence allegedly involving Awami League activists in different parts of the country.
The meeting began at around 2:30pm, with Prime Minister and Leader of the House Tarique Rahman in the chair, on the final day of the current session of parliament, said Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
BNP parliamentary party members attended the meeting.
Talking to UNB, several BNP MPs said the recent violence in Gopalganj and some other parts of the country would come up for discussion, along with the party's next course of action.
Party sources said the meeting would also discuss the party's parliamentary activities and other issues.

item.title: 29 candidates submit nomination papers for Red Crescent Managing Board election
item.description:
A total of 29 candidates submitted their nomination papers to contest the Managing Board election of the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (for the 2026–2028 term).
At the society's national headquarters, candidates submitted their nomination papers against their respective posts within the scheduled time.
On Tuesday, 33 candidates collected nomination papers to participate in the managing board election.
Under the sincere initiative of the society's chairman Barrister Md Abdus Salam, electoral activities are progressing according to the announced schedule to ensure a free, fair, transparent, neutral, and participatory election.
With the submission of nomination papers by aspiring candidates, the electoral process has moved one step forward.
According to the election schedule, scrutiny of nomination papers and publication of the preliminary list of nominated candidates will take place tomorrow, November 19.
Appeals against the scrutiny decisions will be accepted on November 20, followed by appeal hearings and settlements on November 21.
The Election Commission will publish the list of validly nominated candidates on November 22, and the final list of contesting candidates on November 23 following the withdrawal of candidacies.
Notably, the managing board election of the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society will be held on November 25.
Results will be announced on the same day after the conclusion of voting.

item.title: Sony launches next-gen TVs, home audio system in Bangladesh
item.description:
World-renowned Japanese brand Sony has officially launched its latest cutting-edge televisions and sound system for consumers in Bangladesh.
The new lineup includes the flagship Bravia 9 II True RGB TV, the Bravia3 II series, and the Bravia Theatre Trio wireless home audio system.
The products were unveiled at a ceremony on Wednesday (November 18) at the Hotel Intercontinental, Dhaka, inaugurated by Yap Yung, head of marketing, RMDC Sony Southeast Asia.
The event was attended by Joshua Quek, head of Bangladesh Branch, Sony International (Singapore) Ltd; and Kemnuj Maschavalit, manager, TV Product Marketing, RMDC Sony Southeast Asia, among others.
Developed around the "Cinema is Coming Home" concept, these products are designed to bring theater-like picture and sound quality right into the living room.
Crafted with insights from filmmakers and sound engineers at Hollywood's Sony Pictures Entertainment, these devices allow viewers to experience visuals and audio true to the creators' original intent.
Sony’s new flagship model, the Bravia 9 II, introduces 'True RGB LED' technology for the first time.
Unlike conventional TVs, it independently controls red, green, and blue primary light sources, resulting in more vibrant, bright, and accurate colors on screen.
The TV will be available in two large sizes: 85 inches and 115 inches.
Along with ensuring clear visuals from any angle in the room, the 85-inch model features a special anti-glare screen that prevents light reflections even in brightly lit rooms.
It also comes equipped with Gemini AI-powered Google TV and specialized audio technology for crystal-clear dialogue.
Meanwhile, to bring advanced technology within reach of everyday consumers, Sony has introduced the Bravia 3 II series.
This TV will be available in seven different sizes, ranging from 43 inches to 100 inches.
Powered by Sony’s specialized XR Processor, it automatically upscales standard-definition video close to 4K quality.
Alongside watching movies, it offers high-speed gaming features tailored for sports and video games.
Additionally, support for Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos brings extra depth to both picture and sound.
To deliver sound that matches large-screen TVs, Sony has launched the Bravia Theatre Trio, a three-speaker wireless sound system.
Using specialized technology, these three speakers create a surround-sound sensation equivalent to 24 speakers filling the room.
Furthermore, with the help of a small included microphone, the system can detect the room's acoustics and automatically calibrate the sound.
It also allows users to connect wireless subwoofers directly to compatible Bravia TVs without needing an additional soundbar.
Keeping the environment in mind, recycled plastic has been used in the body and remote controls of these new TVs.
Additionally, to ensure ease of use for people of all ages, the buttons on the remote control have been designed to be clearer and more accessible.
The new TVs and audio system will be available at the showrooms of Sony’s official distributors in Bangladesh, Sony Smart and Sony Rangs.
Both organizations will soon announce the official pricing and retail launch dates for these products.

item.title: CPD for raising RMG workers’ minimum wage between Tk18,578 and Tk24,204
item.description:
The Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) on Wednesday proposed setting the minimum wage for readymade garment (RMG) workers between Tk18,578 and Tk24,204, considering the rising cost of living and inflation.
According to the organization, an RMG worker needs a monthly wage of Tk24,204 to cover food, housing, healthcare, education, and other basic needs for a four-member family, alongside a modest margin for savings.
These proposals from a research report were presented at a press conference Wednesday (November 18), at CPD’s office in the capital.
CPD executive director Nazneen Ahmed presented the keynote paper at the event.
Distinguished Fellows Dr Debapriya Bhattacharya and Prof Mustafizur Rahman, along with research director Towfiqul Islam Khan, were also present.
In its study, CPD outlined three potential wage tiers based on the cost of living.
First, to maintain the current market purchasing power of the Tk12,500 minimum wage set in November 2023, the wage would need to be Tk16,351.
However, this amount would not improve workers’ living standards—it would merely preserve their previous purchasing power.
Second, a single earner requires a monthly income of Tk18,578 to meet the minimum expenses needed to stay above the upper poverty line for a four-member family.
Finally, Tk24,204 is required to ensure a decent standard of living that covers food, housing, healthcare, education, and other basic necessities while allowing for small savings.
Nazneen Ahmed said they are proposing a minimum wage for garment workers within the range of Tk18,578 to Tk24,204, considering the current cost of living.
She stated that amid ongoing economic and global pressures, wage determination should not rely on imposition or confrontational processes, but rather on concrete data and evidence.
She noted that the traditional practice of hastily forming a wage board in the face of labor unrest or protests fails to resolve crises in the long term.
In November 2023, the minimum wage for garment workers was fixed at Tk12,500.
Subsequently, in October this year, workers took to the streets demanding a minimum wage of Tk30,000, prompting the government to form a six-member wage board.
Workers' representatives have proposed a minimum wage of Tk32,000 to the board, while factory owners have yet to submit a specific figure.
Highlighting the positions of both workers and owners on wage setting, Nazneen Ahmed noted that owners cite high inflation, steep bank loan interest rates, gas and electricity shortages, rising production costs, and falling apparel prices in global markets—including the United States—as reasons they struggle to absorb higher wage burdens.
Conversely, workers argue that given the sharp rise in food and housing costs, wages must be sufficient to cover essential living expenses.
Nazneen Ahmed further said: “We believe that over time, our goal should be to move workers toward a living wage—ensuring a wage that enables them to maintain proper nutrition and live a humane, dignified life. This broader objective must be taken into account when determining wages.”
“We do not want to use the word ‘bargaining’; rather, we are advocating for determining an acceptable wage between Tk18,578 and Tk24,204 through mutual review and dialogue between both parties,” she added.
Recommendations
CPD also put forward several recommendations to ensure lasting industrial peace and maintain international competitiveness in the apparel sector.
These include forming the wage board at least six months prior to a wage review, basing wage decisions on reliable data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) rather than emotion or pressure, and factoring in the actual household size and number of earners per worker family.
Additionally, the organization recommended developing specific methodologies to measure the 11 criteria outlined in Section 141 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006—such as inflation, productivity, and business capacity.
CPD also urged international buyers and brands to offer fair prices and adjust their sourcing policies in line with rising labor costs.
According to the think tank, in the context of Bangladesh’s graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category by 2029, maintaining competitiveness in major export markets, including the European Union, is critical.
At the same time, to prepare for securing GSP Plus facilities, garment factories must ensure decent working conditions and a living wage for workers.

item.title: ADB deepens support to mobilize private investment in Bangladesh
item.description:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has reaffirmed its commitment to helping Bangladesh attract long-term private investment, diversify its economy, and expand sustainable infrastructure financing.
During November 16-18, ADB Director General (DG) for South Asia Sona Shrestha led a One-ADB delegation to Dhaka for high-level discussions with government, regulatory, private sector, and development partners.
The delegation included Takeo Koike, head of ADB’s Office of Markets Development and Public–Private Partnership, and Craig Lee Roberts, senior adviser in ADB’s Private Sector Operations Department.
“Bangladesh’s next phase of growth will require deeper financial markets, a stronger investment climate, and reforms that enable private enterprise to invest, innovate, and create jobs,” said DG Shrestha.
“ADB will continue to bring together its public and private sector expertise to help translate the country’s development priorities into bankable investments.”
The delegation discussed banking, taxation, and state-owned enterprise reforms; development of bond and equity markets; and wider access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises with Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Masud Khan, Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tanvir Shahriar Ghani.
During the visit, the Finance and Planning Minister joined ADB in launching PPP Monitor: Bangladesh, which uses more than 500 indicators to identify barriers to private investment in infrastructure.
ADB also signed an agreement to extend its transaction advisory support to five additional solar and battery storage projects.
The expanded pipeline now covers six projects with more than 1,000 megawatts of planned capacity and is expected to help mobilize over $1 billion in private investment.
Discussions with businesses and development partners will also inform the master plan for Bangladesh’s Integrated Growth Network Development initiative and ADB’s country partnership strategy for 2028–2032.

item.title: Top Glove offers Bangladeshi workers opportunity via zero-cost ethical recruitment
item.description:
Malaysia-based multinational company Top Glove Sdn. Bhd. is offering Bangladeshi workers an opportunity to secure overseas employment through a 100% zero-cost recruitment model, aimed at ensuring transparent, ethical and financially secure recruitment.
As one of the world's leading glove manufacturers, Top Glove provides employment opportunities, structured working environments and prospects for long-term employment to workers from different countries.
The key feature of this initiative is that workers are not required to pay recruitment fees to secure employment.
Recruitment-related expenses are to be borne by the employer, helping protect workers from excessive charges, intermediaries and financial exploitation.
The approach is consistent with the responsible recruitment principles promoted by the International Labour Organization (ILO).
Overseas employment is an important source of income for many Bangladeshi families.
However, high recruitment costs have traditionally placed considerable financial pressure on workers and their families.
Top Glove's employer-funded recruitment model offers an opportunity to demonstrate that international employment can be arranged without transferring recruitment costs to workers.
The initiative could also establish a positive precedent for Bangladesh–Malaysia manpower cooperation.
The recruitment initiative has attracted negative reactions and criticism on social media and in certain media outlets.
While transparency, accountability and workers' welfare deserve scrutiny, criticism should remain factual, fair and proportionate.
Concerns regarding selection procedures, recruitment transparency and workers' rights should be addressed openly.
However, judging the entire initiative solely on the basis of operational difficulties during interview arrangements may overlook its broader employment objectives.
Unfair or misleading publicity could also discourage international employers from considering Bangladesh for future recruitment opportunities.
The interview arrangements encountered some difficulties. Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) was responsible for the interview venue, coordination and security arrangements.
However, the process did not proceed as smoothly as expected, creating operational challenges and affecting the overall interview experience.
Such shortcomings should encourage all stakeholders to review the process, improve institutional coordination and ensure professional arrangements for future recruitment exercises rather than focusing solely on assigning blame.
The success of zero-cost recruitment requires coordinated efforts from the employer, Bangladesh Government, BOESL and relevant recruitment and training partners. Clear responsibilities, effective communication, proper documentation and transparent selection procedures are essential.
Most importantly, no agent, sub-agent, intermediary or unauthorized individual should demand payment from candidates under this program.
Top Glove's initiative offers an opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh–Malaysia employment cooperation while promoting ethical recruitment and migrant worker protection.
For Bangladeshi workers, it represents the prospect of employment with an established international company without the burden of recruitment costs.
For Top Glove, Bangladesh remains a potential source of capable and hardworking employees.
Rather than allowing operational challenges or negative publicity to overshadow the initiative, stakeholders should work together to strengthen the recruitment process, protect workers' interests and encourage responsible international employers.

item.title: HSBC highlights cybersecurity, digital resilience for organizational preparedness
item.description:
The Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Bangladesh recently organized Cyber Security and Digital Resilience events for its corporate customers in Dhaka and Chattogram.
The events brought together Chief Financial Officers (CFOs), Chief Technology Officers (CTOs) and other senior representatives from different corporate clients and key stakeholders to discuss the evolving cyber threat landscape and the importance of strengthening organizational preparedness.
The sessions highlighted the growing complexity of cyber threats and the need for businesses to develop robust capabilities to identify, prevent and respond to potential risks.
Discussions also focus on the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI), which, while creating new opportunities for business and innovation, is also enabling cybercriminals to launch more sophisticated, targeted and scalable attacks.
The rise of AI-generated impersonations, deepfakes and increasingly convincing phishing attempts makes digital vigilance and resilience more important than ever.
Todd Stewart, chief information security officer, International Markets, HSBC, delivered the keynote address, highlighting the importance of digital transformation and data protection.
He said: “It was so remarkable to see the level of genuine interest and engagement from the audience, which really showed how Cyber Security is at the front of everyone’s mind. HSBC is continuing to prioritize investment in Cyber Security ensuring that we can stay ahead of the emerging threats and protect our customers well into the future.”
He also highlighted HSBC’s continued investment in digital innovation and its efforts to strengthen protection for clients against associated cyber risks and continues to enhance its cybersecurity capabilities through multiple layers of security controls, round-the-clock security monitoring, cyber intelligence and threat analysis, and continuous improvements in its ability to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from cyber threats.
HSBC continues to leverage its extensive global network, advanced digital platforms and deep market expertise to help businesses navigate complexity, strengthen resilience and unlock new opportunities for sustainable growth.

item.title: DU to appeal HC order suspending admission tests until Dec 31
item.description:
The University of Dhaka (DU) has decided to appeal a High Court (HC) order suspending admission tests at all public universities until December 31, warning that a delay could disrupt the academic calendar and leave students facing session backlogs.
DU Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration) Professor Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane announced the decision on Wednesday, saying the university had been informed of the court order.
He said DU’s admission schedule was coordinated with those of other public universities, making a last-minute postponement difficult. As preparations are already underway to hold exams in divisional cities, rescheduling and completing the process could take until March.
DU legal adviser Kazi Mohammad Zainal Abedin told Dhaka Tribune that the university had taken a policy decision to challenge the order. He said DU, an autonomous institution under the 1973 Order, had the authority to make decisions in the interests of its students.
Earlier on Wednesday, a High Court bench comprising Justices Ahmed Sohel and SM Iftikhar Uddin Mahmud ordered all public universities to suspend admission tests until December 31 following a writ petition.
The petitioner, lawyer Kamrun Nahar Mahmuda, argued that students who failed this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations had been given an opportunity to sit supplementary tests, with results scheduled for December 23.
She said DU’s admission tests, scheduled to begin on December 5, could prevent students who pass the supplementary exams from competing for admission.
The University Grants Commission (UGC) had earlier asked DU to reconsider its schedule, proposing that admission applications open in January and coordinated tests begin in February, after the publication of re-evaluation and supplementary exam results.
However, at an emergency meeting on November 9, DU’s general admission committee decided to retain its original schedule. The university’s admission tests are set to run from December 5 to 26.

item.title: Youth hacked to death for filming gang attack in Narayanganj
item.description:
A 25-year-old man was hacked to death in Fatullah of Narayanganj for recording a gang attack on his mobile phone on Tuesday night.
The victim, Yusuf Molla, was attacked around 8pm in the Shiachar Takkar Math area. He died while undergoing treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital around 12:30 am. Yusuf, son of Mofiz Molla from Berki village in Chandpur, worked as a driver and lived in a rented house in the area.
According to locals, a group of 40-50 armed men attacked the house of Delwar Hossain Delu, a BNP member from Ward 9 of Kutubpur union, vandalising the property. The attackers were carrying machetes, knives and other locally made weapons.
Yusuf, who lived in a neighbouring house, was filming the attack when the assailants noticed him and tried to seize his phone. As he resisted, they hacked him indiscriminately before fleeing. His family first took him to Khanpur 300-bed Hospital before transferring him to Dhaka Medical College Hospital as his condition deteriorated.
Delu alleged that the attack stemmed from an earlier dispute involving local Krishak Dal leader Jewel Arman, who had allegedly extorted Tk8 lakh from him in June. A case over the incident is pending in court.
Narayanganj Additional Superintendent of Police Mohammad Shamim Hossain said the attack followed a clash between the two groups earlier in the day. He confirmed that Yusuf was attacked for filming the incident and said legal action would be taken against those involved.

item.title: Cyclone Akvan leaves fishermen stranded as Bay turns rough
item.description:
Barely days after the previous storm disrupted fishing activities, another cyclone, Akvan, has formed over the southwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining west-central Bay, prompting authorities to hoist distant warning Signal No 2 at all four seaports.
The rough sea has left fishermen in distress, particularly those who ventured into the deep sea for fishing. Many have been forced to take shelter on different islands and shoals around Dublar Char near the Sundarbans estuary. The disruption has also brought dry fish production to a near standstill, leaving workers at the island's fishing settlements struggling to make ends meet.
With another cyclone forming just 12 days after the previous one, the Bay has turned rough once again. Unable to withstand the turbulent conditions in deep waters, fishermen have returned to nearby islands and coastal areas, disrupting fishing activities and threatening their seasonal earnings.
Several low-pressure systems and depressions, along with three cyclones, have formed over the Bay of Bengal this year. Cyclone Arnab developed over the central Bay on October 24 and made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28. Fishermen had just begun arriving in Dublar Char for the dry fish season when the storm disrupted their activities.
Another cyclone, Murashu, hit the southern Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3, further delaying fishing. A low-pressure system formed on November 13 and intensified into a depression on November 15 before developing into Cyclone Akvan on November 17-18. The storm is moving towards India's Andhra Pradesh coast.
Several other low-pressure systems and depressions also formed over the Bay in January, July, August and September.
Md Khalilur Rahman, acting officer-in-charge of the Dublar Char Forest Office, said fishermen had faced repeated setbacks since the beginning of the dry fish season.
Their journey to Dublar Char was delayed by Cyclone Arnab on October 30, followed by another disruption caused by Cyclone Murashu on November 3. Before even 15 days of the season had passed, Cyclone Akvan struck again, he said.
"Fishermen cannot venture into the sea because of the rough weather. They are also unable to dry fish on the platforms. As a result, they are spending idle days and suffering financial losses," he said.
Many fishermen are now struggling with debts and uncertainty, while the decline in dry fish production could also affect the Forest Department's revenue, he added.
According to a special weather bulletin issued by the Bangladesh Meteorological Department on Wednesday morning, Cyclone Akvan had intensified into a severe cyclonic storm over the southwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining west-central Bay.
At 6am on November 18, its centre was located 1,280km southwest of Chittagong, 1,220km southwest of Cox's Bazar, 1,185km southwest of Mongla and 1,170km southwest of Payra seaports.
The storm was moving north-northwestwards and was likely to cross India's Andhra Pradesh coast around noon on November 20 as a severe cyclonic storm.
The maximum sustained wind speed near its centre was 89kmph, with gusts reaching up to 117kmph. The sea remained very rough near the storm's centre.
The meteorological department advised fishing boats and trawlers in the North Bay to remain close to the coast and navigate with caution until further notice.
Despite the warning, coastal areas of Khulna, Bagerhat and Satkhira experienced intermittent sunshine and cloudy conditions on Wednesday. Water levels in local rivers were slightly higher than normal, although river transport remained unaffected. The deep sea, however, remained rough.
Shankar Kumar Bihari, a fisherman taking shelter on Dublar Char, said they had faced repeated disruptions since arriving for the dry fish season.
"We were caught in Cyclone Arnab at the beginning of the season. Before even 15 days had passed, Akvan struck again. We have now left the sea and taken shelter on the island," he said.
He added that July had also been difficult for fishermen because of successive low-pressure systems. Although conditions improved briefly in early August, two consecutive low-pressure systems disrupted fishing again.
Whenever adverse weather makes the sea rough, fishermen are forced to return from deep waters, affecting their catches and income.
Earlier, three consecutive low-pressure systems formed over the Bay in July, one of which developed into a monsoon depression and another into a deep depression.
A low-pressure system also formed over the North Bay and adjoining West Bengal-Bangladesh coast on August 12. It subsequently intensified into a well-marked low-pressure system and then a land depression before weakening. Another low-pressure system formed on August 16, prolonging the difficulties for fishermen.

item.title: 45 young people showcase CHT stories through mobile video workshop
item.description:
Forty-five young people from the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) have showcased stories about their communities through mobile videos produced during a three-day storytelling workshop in Rangamati.
Titled “Voices from the Hills”, the workshop concluded on Tuesday with a screening of participants’ videos highlighting local culture, livelihoods, challenges and resilience.
Organised by the Department of Journalism, Media and Communication at Daffodil International University (DIU), with support from UNDP Bangladesh’s ERRD-CHT Project, the workshop brought together participants from Rangamati, Khagrachhari and Bandarban.
The closing event was held at the Tourism Holiday Complex in Rangamati, where participants screened their completed videos and exchanged experiences with trainers and fellow participants.
On the final day, participants completed editing their footage, interviews and photographs under the guidance of trainers. They also received practical instruction on storytelling, shot selection, audio quality, captions and titles.
The workshop began on Sunday with sessions on storytelling techniques, human-centred story selection, storyboarding, mobile videography and video editing.
On Monday, participants visited communities in Rangamati to collect stories through interviews, photographs and video footage. Their work covered education, livelihoods, climate change, women's participation, youth aspirations, culture and environmental issues.
The training also emphasised informed consent, cultural sensitivity and respect for people's dignity when documenting and sharing community stories.
The sessions were facilitated by Dr Md Abdul Kabil Khan, associate professor and head of DIU's Department of Journalism, Media and Communication; Lecturer Meherun Nahar; and Lecturer Md Tanvir Rahman, with support from other department members.
Speaking at the closing session, Shareful Hassan, planning, monitoring and reporting analyst at UNDP Bangladesh's ERRD-CHT Project, said communities were experiencing changes in their everyday lives alongside technological and lifestyle transformations.
He stressed the importance of preserving local culture and heritage amid these changes.
Meher Nigar Bhuiyan, programme manager of the European Union's Resilient Livelihoods Programme, encouraged young people to use their creativity and skills to highlight everyday challenges, particularly the untold stories of marginalised communities in the CHT.
She expressed hope that the workshop would inspire further storytelling initiatives and help bring local experiences to a wider audience.
Supported by the European Union, the ERRD-CHT Project works across the three hill districts to promote inclusive education, climate resilience, biodiversity conservation, good governance, social cohesion and youth engagement.
The workshop aimed to strengthen young people's storytelling skills and amplify local voices through mobile video production.

item.title: Bangladesh edge past Macau in AFC U-17 Asian Cup qualifiers
item.description:
Bangladesh U-17 national football team recorded their second victory in the 2027 AFC U-17 Asian Cup qualification when they edged past Macau by a solitary goal held on Tuesday at Saud Bin Saqr Al Qasimi Stadium in Ras Al Khaimah, United Arab Emirates (UAE).
With this win, Bangladesh secured six points from three matches while Macau remained with their previous collection of three points playing four matches.
In the day's match, Mustakim scored the all-important goal for Bangladesh early in the 18th minute of the match and they maintained the lead till the final whistle.
Bangladesh will play their crucial final group match UAE on November 20 at Emirates Football Club Stadium, Ras Al Khaimah.
Earlier, Bangladesh began their campaign with a 5-1 goal defeat to Syria in their opening group stage match but staged a brilliant fight back to register a convincing 4-0 victory over Bhutan in their second group match.
Only the champions team of the group will qualify in the final round.

item.title: Turning down the noise
item.description:
We appreciate the High Court Division issuing a set of interim directives to curb noise pollution in the capital -- ordering regular drives in silent zones, strict regulation of unnecessary honking, and the creation of a dedicated complaint hotline.
It is safe to say, however, that given the authorities' chronic failure to enforce existing noise laws, these latest directives only have meaning should they see implementation.
For the tens of millions of residents of Dhaka, which is routinely ranked the most noise-polluted city on Earth, having meaningful judicial intervention is long overdue.
Every day, citizens endure an unrelenting acoustic assault, from illegal hydraulic horns, unregulated construction, and blaring loudspeakers. Even designated silent zones -- within 100 metres of hospitals, schools, and courts, as well as around Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and the Secretariat -- remain completely indistinguishable from chaotic traffic intersections.
Bangladesh has never suffered from a shortage of laws or court orders; it suffers from a terminal paralysis of enforcement.
Regulators have long been armed with clear mandates but what has been missing is institutional will. Too often, enforcement amounts to theatrical, one-day mobile court drives for television cameras, followed immediately by business as usual.
The High Court's requirement that relevant ministries and agencies submit compliance reports every three months provides a crucial accountability mechanism, and it must be taken seriously. Judicial directives only matter when backed by relentless, everyday execution.
Dhaka continues to rank near the bottom of global liveability indexes, and its noise pollution is a major reason for this. The citizens of the capital have a right to peace, health, and sanity, and curbing our noise pollution levels is one way to move in the right direction.

item.title: Law enforcement requires genuine reform
item.description:
We are sceptical about the latest wave of administrative changes -- including the abrupt transfer of five senior officials in Gopalganj following violent unrest, the relocation of 100 police personnel from Cox's Bazar over alleged narcotics links, and the withdrawal of Chuadanga’s deputy commissioner -- that have once again placed Bangladesh’s law enforcement and civil administration under intense public scrutiny.
While the authorities concerned frame these moves as routine oversight and accountability, senior analysts and legal experts have rightly warned that knee-jerk transfers, forced retirements, and ad-hoc reappointments are not substitutes for genuine institutional reform.
For decades, this country’s policing apparatus has been hollowed out by deep-seated institutional rot, partisan instrumentalization, and a pervasive culture of impunity.
Simply shuffling officers from one district to another when security lapses occur does nothing to fix the wave of systemic failures. Indeed, all it does is merely export incompetence or misconduct to a new area.
Worse still, relying on opaque withdrawals and arbitrary sackings without transparent, evidence-based inquiries breeds fear, paralysis, and mistrust, leaving honest officers hesitant to act decisively.
To describe rampant corruption, intelligence failures, and violent breakdowns in law and order as mere "isolated incidents" is also an exercise in dangerous denial.
Cosmetic reshuffles and intensified internal surveillance cannot cure a force still governed by an archaic, colonial-era command structure that prioritizes political obedience over public service.
If the government is serious about restoring public trust and building a professional, dependable police force, it must abandon reactive firefighting and execute structural overhaul.
Transparency has never been a word associated with our law enforcement nor the government itself, but it is what is needed if we are to see any meaningful change.

item.title: IAEA: US Saudi nuclear agreement 'satisfactory'
item.description:
UN nuclear watchdog head Rafael Grossi on Wednesday welcomed a deal between the United States and Saudi Arabia on equipping the kingdom with a civilian nuclear program.
The deal announced in July has provoked questions about the risks of nuclear proliferation.
"It's a very satisfactory outcome that we have with this agreement," Grossi told reporters after opening an International Atomic Energy Agency board of governors' meeting.
Once nuclear power development gets under way in Saudi Arabia, "we will be there," he added.
In his opening statement, Grossi told the board that the United States and Saudi Arabia in October requested the IAEA "to take the necessary steps to implement safeguards and verification measures" for their agreement.
According to the accord, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Grossi said.
"I welcome the open, transparent approach and engagement of both governments with member states and the secretariat on this matter," he added.
Grossi told reporters the agreement was "fully aligned with the legal framework that we have at the IAEA."
He added Saudi Arabia had also agreed to "additional verification measures on a voluntary basis."
US media have reported the agreement would allow Washington to export technology without the usual safeguards preventing future military use.
US President Donald Trump said just after the agreement was signed in July that it depended on Saudi Arabia recognizing Israel.

item.title: ‘Human’ is Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year
item.description:
“Human,” meaning to have the “qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines” has been named Cambridge Dictionary’s Word of the Year.
In an era of rapidly expanding Artificial Intelligence (AI) and dire warnings it could even wipe out humanity, the word captured “the 2026 zeitgeist,” Cambridge University Press board member Francesca Woodward told AFP.
Over the past 12 months, she said, people had been “really considering what it is to be human” in particular due to concerns about AI taking over their jobs.
“I think people are trying to remind themselves of ... what human means,” she said.
The word beat off competition from other words related to AI and the online world, reflecting intense global interest in how technology is changing our lives, she said.
The dictionary’s lexicographers had also observed an increased used of “human” in compound words such as human-made or human author, she added.
Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, described “human” as a “really interesting choice ... because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.”
“We’re trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we’re creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?” he said.
The focus on what it means to be human has seen global leaders and prominent figures such as Pope Leo XIV, Bill Gates, classicist Mary Beard and actor Cate Blanchett weigh in on the debate.
Other contenders for the word of the year crown included “agent, meaning an artificial intelligence system that can operate in a complicated way without human control.
Also in the running was “wholesome,” defined as “good for you, and likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.”
“Dusking” was also in contention, the practice of watching daylight turn to darkness as a form of relaxation.
A Dutch tradition, it has been revived as a way of reconnecting with the natural world.
Other new words added to the dictionary in 2026 included “aura farming”, doing things to show a personality that people will admire, and “looksmaxing,” making yourself as physically attractive as possible.
The word of the year and new additions are selected using a range of criteria including the words searched for on the Cambridge Dictionary website.
Among words to watch for next year, according to Cambridge Dictionary, were Fobo, “fear of becoming obsolete” because your job can be performed by AI.
Another was “weather whiplash”, denoting a “quick change from one extreme of weather to another”.
Last year’s word of the year was “parasocial” to describe the sense of having a connection to a famous person you do not know personally or a fictional character.

item.title: Explosion heard in Saudi capital, missiles intercepted
item.description:
A powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh on Wednesday, AFP journalists and residents said, as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis pressed their campaign of attacks against the kingdom.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said they intercepted two cruise missiles -- the latest in weeks of strikes targeting military, civilian and oil infrastructure.
Residents said Wednesday’s explosion came without warning, with no mobile-phone alert issued beforehand as is usually the case during aerial threats.
“The explosion was extremely loud,” said a resident in northern Riyadh. “Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening.”
An AFP journalist said doors throughout her home swung open and the lights briefly went out.
The location of the explosion was not immediately clear, but residents told AFP they saw smoke near Riyadh’s airport in the northeast of the city.
In October, a deadly attack targeting Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.
Within minutes, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the group towards the Riyadh region.
Earlier, the coalition had reported intercepting another cruise missile also heading for the same region.
Saudi civil defense authorities also said they had activated early warning systems in the southern regions of Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border.
The Saudi-led coalition, which backs neighboring Yemen’s internationally recognized government in its war with the Houthis, has battled a surge in attacks since hostilities reignited in July.
The long-running civil war in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, had been largely dormant after a ceasefire went into effect in 2022.
The Houthis are now nearing Aden, the government’s interim capital, having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed.
Since the summer, more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced by the fighting, according to the United Nations.

item.title: Gulf countries under fire after US hits Iran island
item.description:
Gulf nations scrambled to intercept incoming fire on Wednesday, after Iran and its allies lashed out following a US strike on a strategic island, in attacks that threatened to derail efforts to end the war.
Kuwait activated its air defenses to counter drone strikes -- the first since early September -- and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack, after the United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the flashpoint Strait of Hormuz.
Explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude oil exporter, which said it intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Iran-backed Houthis, who have been seizing fresh territory in neighboring Yemen.
Bahrain has now suffered four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic on February 28.
Iran responded by striking America’s wealthy Gulf allies, which host US military bases, and blockading Hormuz, which before the war carried a quarter of global oil flows.
The Iranian army said “combat and kamikaze drones” targeted US air defense systems and launch platforms at Kuwait’s Ali Al-Salem air base on Wednesday.
A day earlier, American fighter jets hit a missile launch site on Qeshm Island with “precision munitions,” a US military official said, describing it as a riposte to Iranian aggression.
Iran’s army chief Amir Hatami warned of a “more devastating” reaction to America and its allies.
“Should the enemy make a mistake and repeat actions that have previously led them to despair, our response -- directed at both the enemy and their backers -- will undoubtedly be even more devastating and will know no geographical boundaries,” Hatami said, according to Iran’s Fars news agency.
Mediator Qatar, which held talks with Iranian officials on Tuesday, called the latest attacks a “dangerous escalation” and warned they undercut efforts to find a peaceful solution.
“The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that could complicate efforts to contain tensions and undermine political and diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring the security and stability of the region,” a foreign ministry statement said.
Kuwaiti residents described feelings of foreboding as attacks returned to the tiny, oil-rich country, which was hit hard by Iranian strikes earlier in the war.
“The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying,” said Egyptian resident Hani Mohammed, 40.
“People had started to readjust to a normal life. The sounds of planes and explosions no longer set the pace of daily life as before. But what happened has revived feelings of anxiety.”
Meanwhile, one seafarer was missing after a ship belonging to Adnoc, the United Arab Emirates’ oil giant, was struck late on Tuesday in Hormuz, the company said.
Ships transiting Hormuz have come under nearly daily fire from Iran, which insists they use routes it has authorized.
The US has responded by imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, and its navy escorts tankers through the narrow passage.
Saudi Arabia has endured weeks of attacks by the Houthis, who have completed their control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and advanced close to the government’s interim capital, Aden.
A four-year truce in Yemen’s bloody civil war, where a Saudi-led coalition has fought for the government since 2015, dissolved in July.
On Wednesday, an “extremely loud” explosion was heard in the north of the Saudi capital Riyadh, a resident told AFP. Another said windows rattled throughout their house, while doors flew open and lights flickered.
Earlier, Saudi coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X that “a cruise missile, launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Riyadh area, has been intercepted and destroyed.”

item.title: Fears of far-right victory loom over upbeat Paris protest
item.description:
Protesters danced to thumping techno music as 16-year-old Mathieu joined thousands marching through Paris on Tuesday, but beneath the festive atmosphere, fears of a far-right victory in 2027 weighed on him and others in the crowd.
Not yet old enough to vote, Mathieu carried a homemade placard depicting far-right figures, including presidential candidate Marine Le Pen and her deputy Jordan Bardella, beneath the words “End intensive pig farming” scrawled in large black letters.
“The far right coming to power scares me,” the high school student told AFP.
He was among tens of thousands who took to the streets of the French capital in response to a union strike call over the rising cost of living and demands for higher wages for public sector workers.
But beyond their economic grievances, many told AFP they were nervous about the rise of the far-right National Rally and the prospect of Le Pen coming to power next year.
Mathieu, who said he had been attending protests since they began in late September, accused the nationalist, anti-immigration party of trying to soften its image.
“They’re not looking out for us, even though that’s what they want us to believe,” he said.
Le Pen, 58, leads the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron next year, with recent opinion polls putting her support at more than 30 percent.
But while the far right has gained ground across France, it has historically struggled to win support in Paris.
The European Union’s second-largest economy has been rocked by more than a month of high school blockades and protests.
Turnout on Tuesday was lower than at previous demonstrations, AFP journalists observed.
The interior ministry put the number of demonstrators in the capital at 28,000, while unions estimated 175,000.
The atmosphere nevertheless remained carnival-like, with shopping carts laden with ice and one-euro beers rolling through the crowds alongside a sculpture of King Kong clinging to the Eiffel Tower.
For Tahliana Malikite Toure, a 21-year-old university student handing out homemade crepes with friends, the looming presidential election was a source of anxiety.
“I absolutely do not want the RN in power,” she said.
She said she backed hard-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon, who polls show is running second, citing his party’s stance on the environment and its efforts to “fight discrimination.”
Critics accuse Le Pen’s eurosceptic party of remaining fundamentally racist.
Le Pen recently sparked controversy when she told US broadcaster CBS that there was “no discrimination in France” and that it was the “least racist” country, claims disputed by rights groups.
“She’s living on another planet,” Malikite Toure said.
For others, fears about the far right went hand in hand with frustration over Macron’s government.
Astrid Petit, a 43-year-old nurse at a Paris public hospital, marched with a small cardboard sign calling for higher wages.
“There’s a real fear that the RN will come to power,” she said
“But at the same time, we can’t have Macron’s policies continuing. We just can’t.”
For veteran protester Frederique Sandas, 71, the battle was a familiar one.
Sitting on a bench and bobbing her head to the music, she recalled 55 years of taking to the streets against “authoritarianism and the steady deterioration of our social welfare system.”
With another presidential election approaching, she had no intention of stopping.
“We’re still here,” she said, smiling and patting her husband’s knee.

item.title: Five Jubo League, Chhatra League members arrested with bombs in Gazipur
item.description:
Police have arrested five members of the banned Jubo League and Chhatra League in Kaliakair, Gazipur, after recovering petrol bombs and crude bombs from their possession.
They were arrested in front of the Ibn Sina factory in the Safipur area of Kaliakair upazila on Tuesday night.
The arrestees are Abdul Mannan, 45, president of the Tarakanda upazila Jubo League unit in Mymensingh; Biplob Chowdhury, 48, general secretary of the same unit; Miraj Hossain Ifti, 21, joint general secretary of Ward 8 Chhatra League in Kaliakair; Ashik Hossain, 21, deputy secretary for student affairs of the Gazipur district Chhatra League; and Hashem Sikdar, 46, organisational secretary of the Ward 8 Mohalla Awami League in Kaliakair.
Kaliakair police station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said police were on duty in the Safipur area along the Dhaka-Tangail highway on Tuesday night when a group of 60 to 70 members of the banned Jubo League and Chhatra League brought out an unauthorised procession opposing the government.
At around 10:35pm, the group allegedly threw petrol bombs in front of the Ibn Sina factory on the highway. Police chased the procession and arrested five people at the scene.
Police seized five petrol bombs, five crude bombs and remnants of exploded petrol bombs during the operation, the OC said.
He added that a case had been filed against the arrestees under the Anti-Terrorism Act. They were later sent to the Gazipur court, with police seeking a 10-day remand.

item.title: Five Bangladeshi students win medals at Russia’s MY-GEO 2026
item.description:
Bangladesh has jointly secured second place at Russia’s inaugural Multinational Youth Geography Olympiad (MY-GEO 2026), with all five members of its participating team winning individual medals.
The Bangladeshi team won two silver and three bronze medals in the individual competition, marking a notable achievement for the country at the international academic event.
Held from October 24 to 31 in Russia’s Sirius Federal Territory, the Olympiad brought together 11 teams from different countries and regions to compete in geography-related academic and practical challenges.
Russia secured first place, while Bangladesh and Abkhazia jointly finished second. Transnistria, Italy and Pakistan shared third place.
In the individual competition, Tanvir Sadat and Arifa Atiq Mim won silver medals, while Md Tawsikul Islam, Minhajul Islam Tahmid and Shahriar Noor received bronze medals.
The Bangladeshi delegation was led by Taseen Mohammad and Ferdous Ahmed. Ahnaf Tahmid Uddin also accompanied the team as an observer.
The participation of Team Bangladesh was facilitated by the Russian House in Dhaka, which said the initiative reflected its continued efforts to create international educational opportunities for Bangladeshi students and strengthen educational cooperation between Bangladesh and Russia.
According to the organisers, the competition featured theoretical, practical and multimedia stages designed to assess participants’ geographical knowledge, analytical abilities and practical skills.
One of the major highlights was the practical field stage, held on October 28 at the Rosa Khutor Mountain Resort. Participants conducted geographical investigations involving mountain landscapes, including measuring the depth and flow velocity of a mountain river and estimating its water discharge.
They also carried out meteorological observations, measuring air temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure and wind speed.
The students faced additional analytical challenges, including calculating a coffee price index based on distance from ski lifts, demonstrating how geographical knowledge could be applied to real-life situations.
According to the Bangladeshi delegation, the students had undergone special preparations in geography and geology, subjects that are not extensively covered in Bangladesh’s regular school curriculum. Their preparation helped them tackle unfamiliar questions and apply scientific knowledge to different geographical contexts.
Beyond the academic competition, MY-GEO 2026 provided an opportunity for young participants from different countries to exchange knowledge, develop teamwork and build international friendships. Cultural presentations also allowed them to learn about one another’s cultural heritage.
The Russian House in Dhaka said Russia offers various educational opportunities to international students, including those from Bangladesh, through government scholarships, tuition-free higher education, preparatory Russian-language courses and academic exchange programs.
