As the representative office of Russia’s federal agency Rossotrudnichestvo in Bangladesh, the Russian House works to connect Bangladeshi students with Russian universities and educational institutions, provide academic guidance and promote participation in international competitions and scholarship programs.
Bangladesh’s joint second-place finish and the individual medals won by all five team members mark a significant achievement for the country’s young generation, highlighting their potential to compete successfully on international academic and scientific platforms.

item.title: UIU seminar explores lessons from Singapore’s nation-building experience
item.description:
A seminar at United International University (UIU) on Tuesday explored how Singapore transformed itself into a global economic hub and what lessons Bangladesh could draw from its development experience.
The event, titled “Revisiting the Singapore Story: Lessons in Nation Building,” also marked the launch of Singapore: A Nation Building Story, written by UIU Professor Dr Raqibul Mostafa and published by The University Press Limited (UPL).
Organised by UIU’s School of Business and Economics, the seminar brought together diplomats, academics and other guests to discuss the role of leadership, strong institutions, public trust, human capital and long-term planning in Singapore’s development.
Philip Ong, chargé d’affaires ad interim and head of mission at the Singapore High Commission in Dhaka, attended as chief guest and joined the panel discussion.
Ong identified long-term planning, the rule of law, national unity, good governance, an efficient administration and foreign policy as key factors behind Singapore’s progress. He also highlighted the importance of education, human resource development, technology and investment, saying cooperation between the government and the public had contributed to the country’s development.
The book’s author, Mostafa, said his observations during a visit to Singapore for his mother’s medical treatment inspired him to write it. He recalled being impressed by the mutual respect, sense of responsibility, self-reliance and respect for rules among Singaporeans, as well as public trust in the government.
Mahrukh Mohiuddin, managing director of UPL, said the book went beyond documenting Singapore’s development and presented the country’s intellectual and social values, as well as its resilience. She expressed hope that UPL would continue publishing books based on authors’ experiences and observations.
Photo: Courtesy
Md Mustafizur Rahman, former Bangladesh high commissioner to Singapore, said the country placed equal importance on technical and general education. He attributed its development to long-term planning and a merit-based system.
The panel was moderated by Professor Dr M Niaz Asadullah, adviser to UIU’s School of Business and Economics. He highlighted Singapore’s efforts to build national capacity and said Bangladesh and Singapore could benefit from exchanging educational ideas and experiences.
The welcome address was delivered by UIU Registrar Ambassador Dr Md Zulfiqur Rahman. The programme ended with a question-and-answer session attended by students, faculty members, researchers and other guests.

item.title: Five winter favorites that offer more than just great taste
item.description:
As winter approaches, fresh vegetables and seasonal fruits are beginning to fill local markets. From mustard and fenugreek leaves to red carrots, beetroot and locally grown amla, the season offers a variety of nutritious produce. Traditional winter treats such as sesame and jaggery ladoos also become popular during this time.
Beyond their distinctive flavors, these seasonal foods contain essential nutrients that support bone health, immunity, eye health, skin health, and digestion. Adding them to your daily meals can help maintain a balanced diet throughout the colder months.
Here are five seasonal foods worth including in your winter diet.
Mustard and fenugreek leaves are among the most popular leafy vegetables during winter. They are rich in vitamin K, which plays an important role in normal blood clotting and maintaining bone health. They also contain beta-carotene, vitamin C and folate. Beta-carotene is converted into vitamin A in the body, while vitamin C supports the normal functioning of the immune system.
Vitamin C also helps the body absorb iron from plant-based foods. Adding a little lemon juice to cooked leafy vegetables can therefore improve iron absorption. However, it is better to cook them gently rather than overboiling them.
Sesame-based treats, including ladoos, sweets and chutneys, become particularly popular during winter. Despite their small size, sesame seeds are packed with nutrients such as calcium, magnesium, zinc, protein and unsaturated fats. They also contain sesamin, a natural compound that acts as an antioxidant.
Ground sesame seeds can be added to salads, flatbreads and other dishes to increase their nutritional value. However, traditional sesame and jaggery ladoos may contain considerable amounts of added sugar. It is therefore important to enjoy them in moderation.
Amla, also known as Indian gooseberry, is another nutritious addition to the winter diet. This locally available fruit is an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the normal functioning of the immune system. Vitamin C also plays an important role in helping the body absorb iron from plant-based foods.
Amla can be eaten fresh, added to salads or prepared as a chutney with a small amount of spices. However, those who enjoy sweetened preparations such as amla murabba or pickles should be mindful of their sugar content. People with diabetes should be particularly careful about consuming these products.
Fresh red carrots are widely available in local markets during winter. They are rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. This vitamin is essential for maintaining normal vision and healthy skin. Carrots also contain dietary fibre, which supports digestion. Some varieties of red carrots additionally contain lycopene, an antioxidant compound.
Carrots can be eaten raw in salads or included in cooked dishes. Consuming them with a small amount of healthy fat can help the body absorb their carotenoids more efficiently.
Beetroot is another familiar winter vegetable with several nutritional benefits. It contains folate, potassium, dietary fiber and naturally occurring nitrates. Nitrates are converted into nitric oxide in the body, which can help support normal blood vessel function. The fiber in beetroot also contributes to healthy digestion.
Beetroot can be eaten raw in salads, boiled or lightly cooked. However, it is important to remember that eating beetroot alone cannot cure anemia or correct iron deficiency.
Including a variety of seasonal fruits and vegetables in daily meals is important for maintaining good health. Rather than relying on a single food for specific health benefits, it is better to combine leafy greens, fruits, lentils, nuts, whole grains and adequate sources of protein to maintain a balanced diet.
Even nutritious foods should be consumed in appropriate portions. Limiting excessive sugar, salt, and oil while maintaining a varied diet can help support overall health throughout the winter season.

item.title: From glossy lips to bold eyes, give your winter look a stylish makeover
item.description:
Winter brings a shift in beauty trends, and makeup is no exception. Rich shades, dramatic eyes, and statement lips take center stage, but this season's look is not entirely about heavy layers or bold colors. With the weather remaining relatively mild, winter beauty is borrowing a touch of summer's freshness, creating a balance between glamour and a naturally radiant finish.
For makeup enthusiasts, winter offers the perfect opportunity to experiment. Unlike the warmer months, makeup is less likely to wear off quickly, making it easier to explore vibrant colors, layered textures, and more defined looks. This season, however, the emphasis is on making a statement without losing the skin's natural freshness.
Seasonal changes can affect every skin type. Dryness, dullness, and uneven skin tone are common during winter, making skincare an essential part of any makeup routine.
Before applying makeup, gently exfoliate the skin to remove dead cells and follow up with a moisturizer to restore hydration. Well-moisturized skin creates a smoother canvas and helps makeup sit more evenly. Allow the moisturizer around 15 minutes to absorb before moving on to the next step.
Begin with a primer to create an even surface and help makeup last longer. Choosing the right foundation is equally important, particularly if your skin tone has changed since summer.
If you usually prefer matte foundations, winter is a good time to experiment with luminous or satin finishes. A luminous foundation can soften the appearance of dryness while adding a healthy glow. For a lighter, more natural look, a BB or CC cream can be a suitable alternative.
Use concealer to cover dark circles and blemishes, then set the base with pressed powder if needed. Those with oily skin may prefer a matte-finish powder to control excess shine. Add dimension with bronzer, contour, and highlighter, followed by a blush shade that complements your complexion.
Finish with a setting spray to help keep the makeup in place throughout the day.
This season, the eyes offer plenty of room for experimentation. While softer shades are often favored during summer, winter welcomes deeper tones, vibrant eyeshadows, and more dramatic eyeliner.
Experiment with eyeliner along the upper and lower lash lines, switching between fine and bold strokes depending on the look you want. Several coats of mascara can add definition, but colored mascara can also offer an unexpected twist. For a more understated approach, skip mascara occasionally and let eyeshadow and kohl define the eyes instead.
Fuller, slightly untamed eyebrows can also complement the overall look, adding character without appearing overly polished.
Deep lipstick shades continue to dominate winter beauty looks. Burgundy, berry, plum and other rich tones can add depth and sophistication, particularly when paired with winter outfits.
However, nude shades do not have to disappear with the arrival of colder weather. Soft nude and neutral tones can create an elegant contrast with dramatic eye makeup. The key is to avoid shades that make the complexion appear washed out.
Instead of opting exclusively for matte formulas, try creamy or hydrating lipsticks that keep the lips looking smooth. A touch of lip gloss can add dimension and a fresh finish.
Winter also offers more freedom to experiment with hairstyles, whether you prefer leaving your hair loose or styling it to complement your outfit.
A voluminous front puff can add a playful touch, while a sleek, gelled-back style creates a more polished appearance. You can also alternate between straight and curly hairstyles to change the overall mood of your look.
Ultimately, this season's winter beauty aesthetic is about contrast: bold colors balanced with fresh skin, dramatic eyes paired with softer lips, and polished details that still feel effortless. Rather than following a single trend, the best approach is to experiment with textures, colors and finishes while allowing your personal style to take the lead.

item.title: Mintoo: Bangladesh to take carbon credit framework to cabinet this month
item.description:
Bangladesh plans to place its proposed carbon credit framework before the cabinet this month, paving the way for carbon projects, a national registry and access to carbon markets, Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo has said.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, Mintoo said the framework was being finalised after stakeholder consultations. He also outlined plans for tree plantation, plastic waste management and district-specific waste strategies.
Abdul Awal Mintoo: We need a proper framework identifying priority sectors, project implementation procedures, carbon credit management and the establishment of a registry.
I hope to complete it this month. We have held two meetings and will hold another to incorporate stakeholder opinions before placing it before the cabinet.
Abdul Awal Mintoo: We already have MoUs with different organisations and initiatives in agriculture, mangrove-related activities and solar power. We will examine these and take the necessary steps to bring them under the carbon credit mechanism.
Abdul Awal Mintoo: We have already planted around 32.7 million to 32.8 million trees against our target of five million. I will visit the sites after the rainy season to verify the progress. We also have additional saplings and plan to plant them between December 15 and January 30, 2027.
Abdul Awal Mintoo: We are focusing on plastic waste, extended producer responsibility and converting waste into resources. Waste can generate energy, while organic waste can be processed into biofertilisers.
We are considering separate waste management plans for each district, as waste types and quantities vary. I hope to formulate rules by year-end requiring every municipality and city corporation to undertake systematic waste management.

item.title: Dhaka, Colombo agree to establish joint commission to strengthen ties
item.description:
Bangladesh and Sri Lanka on Wednesday signed a document to establish a Joint Consultative Commission for Comprehensive Cooperation to strengthen bilateral relations and institutionalise regular diplomatic engagement at the foreign ministerial level.
The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed in Colombo following a bilateral meeting between State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.
The memorandum of understanding (MoU) aims to create a formal mechanism for consultations on bilateral cooperation and issues of mutual interest.
The commission will facilitate bilateral meetings at the level of foreign ministers, providing a platform for reviewing existing cooperation and exploring opportunities to further strengthen relations between the two countries, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
During the meeting at Sri Lanka's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the two sides discussed recent political developments and economic challenges faced by their respective governments.
They also exchanged views on various initiatives undertaken by both countries to address those challenges.
The ministers expressed satisfaction over the exchange of high-level visits between Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, recognising their importance in strengthening mutual understanding and cooperation.
They underscored the value of continued high-level engagement to review bilateral relations and exchange views on regional and multilateral issues of common concern.
